item.title: Error Handling in R: A Guide for Data Analysts
item.dc:creator: Gutama Girja Urago
item.description:
In the previous post we wrote calc_stats(), a small function that returns the mean and standard deviation of a column. It works well as long as you give it what it expects. Here is what happens when you make a typo in the column name:

calc_stats <- function(data, column) {
  values <- data[[column]]
  data.frame(
    variable = column,
    mean = mean(values, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

calc_stats(mtcars, "mpgg")
Warning in mean.default(values, na.rm = TRUE): argument is not numeric or
logical: returning NA
  variable mean sd
1     mpgg   NA NA

R complains that an argument is “not numeric or logical” and hands back NA instead of numbers. The warning never mentions the real problem, which is that mtcars has no column called mpgg. Worse, the function did not stop, so those NA values can travel into later steps of your analysis. When this happens in the middle of a long script, you can lose a lot of time working out what went wrong.

Error handling is the habit of checking inputs and reporting problems in words that point straight at the cause. This post covers the tools base R gives you for that.

NoteWhat you will learn
  • the difference between errors, warnings and messages, and how R shows each one
  • how to stop a function early with stop() and write messages people can act on
  • quick input checks with stopifnot()
  • when to use warning() and message() instead
  • how to keep a script running when something fails, with try() and tryCatch()

Errors, warnings and messages

R has three ways of telling you something. They look similar in the console, but they mean different things.

An error stops the code. Nothing after it runs, and you get no result:

log("ten")
Error in `log()`:
! non-numeric argument to mathematical function

A warning lets the code finish and return a result, but tells you that something about it may be wrong:

log(-1)
Warning in log(-1): NaNs produced
[1] NaN

R still returned a value (NaN, “not a number”), together with a note that it had to produce one.

A message is plain information. Nothing is wrong; the code is just telling you what it is doing:

message("Reading the household file...")
Reading the household file...

When you write your own functions, you can create all three yourself with stop(), warning() and message().

1. Stopping early with stop()

stop() raises an error with the text you give it. The idea is to check the inputs at the very top of the function, before any real work happens:

divide_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  if (!is.numeric(x) || !is.numeric(y)) {
    stop("Both x and y must be numeric.")
  }
  if (y == 0) {
    stop("Division by zero is not allowed.")
  }
  x / y
}

divide_numbers(10, 2)      # works
[1] 5
divide_numbers(10, "a")    # stops: y is text
Error in `divide_numbers()`:
! Both x and y must be numeric.
divide_numbers(10, 0)      # stops: y is zero
Error in `divide_numbers()`:
! Division by zero is not allowed.

Reading the checks line by line:

  • is.numeric(x) is TRUE when x is a number. The ! in front flips it, so !is.numeric(x) means “x is not a number”.
  • || means “or”. The first if is true when either x or y is not numeric.
  • When an if condition is true, stop() runs and the function ends right there. The division on the last line never happens.

Without these checks, divide_numbers(10, "a") would still fail, but with R’s own message, non-numeric argument to binary operator, which is accurate but not much help to someone who has never seen it before.

Hiding the function call with call. = FALSE

Notice that each error above starts with Error in divide_numbers(10, "a"). R adds the call that failed. That helps while you are writing the function, but for people using it, the message alone is often cleaner:

divide_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  if (!is.numeric(x) || !is.numeric(y)) {
    stop("Both x and y must be numeric.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (y == 0) {
    stop("Division by zero is not allowed.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  x / y
}

divide_numbers(10, "a")
Error:
! Both x and y must be numeric.

2. Writing error messages people can act on

A useful error message answers three questions: what went wrong, why, and what to do about it. Compare:

  • Not helpful: Error in y
  • Helpful: `y` must be a number, but you supplied text ("a").

You can build messages like the second one by pasting in the value you received. Here is calc_stats() from the start of the post, now checking its inputs:

calc_stats <- function(data, column) {
  if (!column %in% names(data)) {
    stop(
      "Column '", column, "' was not found. ",
      "Available columns: ", paste(names(data), collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  values <- data[[column]]
  if (!is.numeric(values)) {
    stop("Column '", column, "' must be numeric.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  data.frame(
    variable = column,
    mean = mean(values, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

calc_stats(mtcars, "mpgg")
Error:
! Column 'mpgg' was not found. Available columns: mpg, cyl, disp, hp, drat, wt, qsec, vs, am, gear, carb

Now the message names the problem and lists the columns you could have meant. stop() pastes all its pieces together, and paste(names(data), collapse = ", ") turns the vector of column names into one comma-separated string.

3. Quick checks with stopifnot()

For simple conditions, writing an if and a stop() for each one gets long. stopifnot() takes a list of conditions and stops at the first one that is not TRUE:

my_mean <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x), length(x) > 0)
  mean(x)
}

my_mean(c(4, 8, 15))
[1] 9
my_mean("a")
Error in `my_mean()`:
! is.numeric(x) is not TRUE

The default message just repeats the condition (is.numeric(x) is not TRUE). Since R 4.0 you can name each condition, and the name becomes the message:

my_mean <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(
    "`x` must be numeric" = is.numeric(x),
    "`x` must contain at least one value" = length(x) > 0
  )
  mean(x)
}

my_mean("a")
Error in `my_mean()`:
! `x` must be numeric

4. Gentle alerts with warning()

Use warning() when the function can still give a sensible answer, but the user should know about something. Taking the log of a vector that contains zeros or negative numbers is a good example: you can return NA for those values and carry on.

Here is a first attempt:

log_value <- function(x) {
  if (any(x <= 0)) {
    warning("Input contains non-positive values; returning NA for those cases.")
  }
  ifelse(x > 0, log(x), NA)
}

log_value(c(1, 10, -3))
Warning in log_value(c(1, 10, -3)): Input contains non-positive values;
returning NA for those cases.
Warning in log(x): NaNs produced
[1] 0.000000 2.302585       NA

The result is right, but there are two warnings, not one. The second one, NaNs produced, comes from log(x). ifelse() computes log() for every value first, including -3, and only then picks which results to keep. So R complains about log(-3) even though that value is thrown away.

The fix is to replace the bad values with NA before taking the log:

log_value <- function(x) {
  if (any(x <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    warning("Input contains zero or negative values; returning NA for those.",
            call. = FALSE)
  }
  log(ifelse(x > 0, x, NA))
}

log_value(c(1, 10, -3))
Warning: Input contains zero or negative values; returning NA for those.
[1] 0.000000 2.302585       NA

Now there is exactly one warning, and it is ours. na.rm = TRUE inside any() makes the check work even when x already contains missing values.

5. Keeping the user informed with message()

message() is for progress updates such as “Reading 12 files…” or “Dropped 3 duplicate rows”. It is better than print() or cat() for this, because whoever calls your function can switch messages off when they do not need them:

clean_ids <- function(ids) {
  dupes <- sum(duplicated(ids))
  message("Dropped ", dupes, " duplicate ID(s).")
  unique(ids)
}

clean_ids(c(101, 102, 102, 103))
Dropped 1 duplicate ID(s).
[1] 101 102 103
suppressMessages(clean_ids(c(101, 102, 102, 103)))
[1] 101 102 103

6. Recovering from failures with try() and tryCatch()

So far we have been raising problems. Sometimes you want the opposite: to catch a problem and keep going. A common case is reading many files in a loop, where one damaged file should not stop the other ninety-nine.

try()

try() runs some code and, if it fails, returns a special “try-error” object instead of stopping:

read_data_safe <- function(path) {
  result <- try(read.csv(path), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(result, "try-error")) {
    warning("Could not read '", path, "'. Check the path and format.",
            call. = FALSE)
    return(NULL)
  }
  result
}

silent = TRUE stops try() from printing the error itself, and inherits(result, "try-error") checks whether the reading failed. Let’s test it on a file that exists and one that does not. tempfile() gives us a temporary file path, so this example does not touch any of your own files:

good_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(head(mtcars, 3), good_file, row.names = FALSE)

read_data_safe(good_file)
   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
1 21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
2 21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
3 22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
read_data_safe("no_such_file.csv")
Warning in file(file, "rt"): cannot open file 'no_such_file.csv': No such file
or directory
Warning: Could not read 'no_such_file.csv'. Check the path and format.
NULL

The first call returns the data. The second returns NULL and the script continues. You see two warnings for it: the first comes from read.csv() itself (it cannot open the file), and the second is ours, which says in plain words what to check.

tryCatch()

tryCatch() gives you more control. You hand it the code to run, plus a separate handler function for each kind of problem:

read_data_robust <- function(path) {
  tryCatch(
    {
      df <- read.csv(path)
      message("File read successfully.")
      df
    },
    error = function(e) {
      message("Error: ", conditionMessage(e))
      NULL
    },
    warning = function(w) {
      message("Warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
      NULL
    },
    finally = {
      message("Finished trying '", basename(path), "'.")
    }
  )
}

How it works:

  • The first block, in { }, is the code you want to run.
  • If that code raises an error, R stops it and runs the error handler instead. The handler receives the error as e, and conditionMessage(e) gives you its text. Whatever the handler returns, here NULL, becomes the result of tryCatch().
  • The warning handler works the same way for warnings. Note that catching a warning also stops the main code, so this function returns NULL even for a small warning. If that is too strict, leave out the warning handler and let warnings pass through.
  • finally runs at the end no matter what happened. It is the place for clean-up, such as closing a connection.

Here it is on three files: a good one, a missing one, and one whose last line has no line ending, which makes read.csv() raise a warning. The long random file names in the output come from tempfile():

odd_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
cat("a,b\n1,2", file = odd_file)   # no newline at the end

read_data_robust(good_file)
File read successfully.
Finished trying 'file492877e412a2.csv'.
   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
1 21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
2 21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
3 22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
read_data_robust("no_such_file.csv")
Warning: cannot open file 'no_such_file.csv': No such file or directory
Finished trying 'no_such_file.csv'.
NULL
read_data_robust(odd_file)
Warning: incomplete final line found by readTableHeader on 'C:\Users\girja\AppData\Local\Temp\Rtmp80Fj8N\file492860dc636.csv'
Finished trying 'file492860dc636.csv'.
NULL

Reading many files without stopping

Look at the missing file. read.csv() first raises a warning (“cannot open file”) and then an error, and since the warning comes first, the warning handler is the one that runs. Handlers react to whichever condition arrives first.

Putting it together, here is the loop that motivated this section. lapply() reads each file, and one bad path does not stop the rest:

paths <- c(good_file, "no_such_file.csv", good_file)
datasets <- suppressWarnings(lapply(paths, read_data_safe))

lengths(datasets)   # number of columns in each result; 0 means it failed
[1] 11  0 11

Which one should I use?

Function Stops the code? Use it when
stop() Yes The input is wrong and no sensible result is possible
stopifnot() Yes You have a few simple conditions to check quickly
warning() No You can return a result, but part of it needs attention
message() No You want to report progress or what the function did
try() No You want to attempt something and check afterwards whether it failed
tryCatch() No You want different responses to errors and warnings, or clean-up with finally

Common mistakes

  • Checking too late. Put input checks at the top of the function. If the function has already done half its work when it fails, it can leave things in a confusing state.
  • Vague messages. “Invalid input” sends the user hunting. Say which argument is wrong and what you expected.
  • Hiding every error. Wrapping everything in tryCatch() and returning NULL makes failures invisible. Catch only the problems you expect, and report them with a warning or message so they are not lost.
  • if with more than one value. if (x == 0) fails with the condition has length > 1 when x is a vector. Use any(x == 0) or all(x == 0) to say what you mean.

Recap

Errors stop the code, warnings let it finish with a caution, and messages are information. Use stop() (or stopifnot() for short checks) at the top of a function to reject bad input with a message that says what went wrong and how to fix it. Use warning() when you can still return something useful, and message() for progress updates. When you need a script to keep running past a failure, try() and tryCatch() let you catch the problem and decide what happens next.

A good place to start is the function you use most. Add two or three checks to it, and the next time something goes wrong, the error will tell you where to look.

item.title: Importance of R Functions: A Guide for Data Analysts
item.dc:creator: Gutama Girja Urago
item.description:
If you have ever copied a block of R code, pasted it further down your script and changed one variable name, you have already met the problem that functions solve. Copy-paste works for a while. Then you fix a mistake in one copy and forget the other two, and the results from different parts of your script no longer agree.

A function lets you write that block once, give it a name, and run it on any input you like. This post walks through how functions work in R, from a two-line example to a grouped summary with dplyr. You only need to know how to run code in RStudio and what a data frame is.

NoteWhat you will learn
  • what a function is and the parts every R function has
  • how arguments, default values and return values work
  • why code inside a function does not change your workspace
  • when it is worth turning code into a function
  • two practical examples: summary statistics for any column, and grouped summaries with dplyr

What is a function?

You use functions all the time already. mean(), sum(), read.csv() and library() are all functions. Each one takes some input, does a job and gives you something back:

mean(c(2, 4, 9))
[1] 5

Here the input is the vector c(2, 4, 9), the job is “add the numbers and divide by how many there are”, and the output is 5. The inputs a function accepts are called arguments, and the thing it hands back is its return value.

Writing your own function means doing the same thing for a job that R does not have a ready-made function for.

Your first function

Here is a function that adds two numbers:

add_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x + y
  return(result)
}

Running this chunk prints nothing. That is expected: you have defined the function, the same way a <- 5 defines a variable without printing it. Line by line:

  • add_numbers <- stores the function under a name, just like any other object in R.
  • function(x, y) says “this is a function, and it takes two arguments called x and y”.
  • Everything between { and } is the body: the code that runs each time you use the function.
  • return(result) sends the value of result back to whoever called the function.

Now you can call it:

add_numbers(5, 2)
[1] 7
add_numbers(x = 10, y = 3)
[1] 13

The second call names the arguments. Both styles work. Naming them makes longer calls easier to read and lets you give them in any order.

You do not always need return()

An R function automatically returns the value of the last line it runs, so this shorter version does exactly the same thing:

add_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  x + y
}

add_numbers(5, 2)
[1] 7

I still use return() in longer functions, because it makes it obvious where the result comes from. In short functions like this one, most R users leave it out.

Default values

You can give an argument a default, which is used when the caller does not supply that argument:

add_numbers <- function(x, y = 10) {
  x + y
}

add_numbers(5)      # y is not given, so the default 10 is used
[1] 15
add_numbers(5, 1)   # y is given, so the default is ignored
[1] 6

You have used defaults without noticing. mean() has an argument na.rm that defaults to FALSE, which is why mean(c(1, NA)) returns NA until you write na.rm = TRUE.

What happens inside a function stays inside

Variables created inside a function exist only while the function runs. They do not appear in your workspace afterwards:

add_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  result <- x + y
  result
}

add_numbers(5, 2)
[1] 7
exists("result")
[1] FALSE

exists("result") is FALSE because result lived inside the function and disappeared when the function finished. This is a good thing. A function cannot accidentally overwrite an object called result that you created somewhere else in your script.

When should you write a function?

A common rule of thumb, from R for Data Science, is to write a function once you have copied and pasted the same block of code more than twice. Look at this:

mean(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 20.09062
sd(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 6.026948
mean(mtcars$hp, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 146.6875
sd(mtcars$hp, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 68.56287
mean(mtcars$wt, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3.21725
sd(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)   # oops: copied from above and not changed to wt
[1] 6.026948

The last line is a real copy-paste bug. It runs without any error and gives you the standard deviation of mpg while you think you are looking at wt. Bugs like this are hard to spot because nothing looks broken.

Turning repeated code into a function helps in three practical ways:

  • One place to fix things. If the calculation needs to change, you change it once.
  • Fewer copy-paste slips. You only type the column name, so there is less to forget.
  • Clearer scripts. A good function name, such as calc_stats(), tells the reader what the code does without making them read every line.

Example 1: mean and standard deviation of any column

Here is the repeated code above, written once as a function:

calc_stats <- function(data, column) {
  mean_val <- mean(data[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_val <- sd(data[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
  list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val)
}

calc_stats(mtcars, "mpg")
$mean
[1] 20.09062

$sd
[1] 6.026948

Two details are worth slowing down for:

  • data[[column]] pulls out one column of a data frame when the column name is stored as text. mtcars[["mpg"]] is the same as mtcars$mpg, but the [[ ]] form works when the name is inside a variable, which is exactly the situation inside a function.
  • list(mean = mean_val, sd = sd_val) returns two values at once by packing them into a named list. You can pull one out with $:
mpg_stats <- calc_stats(mtcars, "mpg")
mpg_stats$mean
[1] 20.09062

A small improvement: return a data frame

A list is fine for one column, but when you summarise several columns you usually want a table. If the function returns a one-row data frame, the results stack neatly:

calc_stats <- function(data, column) {
  values <- data[[column]]
  data.frame(
    variable = column,
    mean = mean(values, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

calc_stats(mtcars, "mpg")
  variable     mean       sd
1      mpg 20.09062 6.026948

Now run it on several columns at once:

columns <- c("mpg", "hp", "wt")
results <- lapply(columns, function(col) calc_stats(mtcars, col))
do.call(rbind, results)
  variable      mean         sd
1      mpg  20.09062  6.0269481
2       hp 146.68750 68.5628685
3       wt   3.21725  0.9784574

lapply() calls calc_stats() once for each column name and collects the three small data frames in a list. do.call(rbind, results) then stacks them into one table. The copy-paste bug from earlier cannot happen here, because each column name is typed exactly once.

Example 2: grouped summaries with dplyr

A very common task in survey work is “give me the mean and standard deviation of this variable for each group”, for example yield by region or income by household type. The dplyr package is built for this.

To have something to work with, let’s create a small made-up dataset. rnorm() draws random numbers from a normal distribution, and set.seed() makes sure you get the same “random” numbers every time you run the code, so your output matches mine:

library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)
scores <- data.frame(
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 5),
  value = rnorm(10)
)

scores
   group       value
1      A -0.56047565
2      A -0.23017749
3      A  1.55870831
4      A  0.07050839
5      A  0.12928774
6      B  1.71506499
7      B  0.46091621
8      B -1.26506123
9      B -0.68685285
10     B -0.44566197

Now the function:

analyze_data <- function(data, group_col, num_col) {
  data |>
    group_by(.data[[group_col]]) |>
    summarize(
      mean_value = mean(.data[[num_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_value = sd(.data[[num_col]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

analyze_data(scores, "group", "value")
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  group mean_value sd_value
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1 A         0.194     0.811
2 B        -0.0443    1.16

What is going on:

  • |> is the pipe. It passes the result of one step into the next, so data |> group_by(...) means “take data, then group it”. You may also see %>% in older code; for this purpose they do the same thing.
  • group_by() splits the data into groups, and summarize() computes one row of results per group.
  • .data[[group_col]] is how you tell dplyr “use the column whose name is stored in group_col”. Inside dplyr you normally write bare column names like group, but here the name arrives as text, so .data[[ ]] does the lookup. It is the dplyr version of data[[column]] from Example 1.

Because the column names are arguments, the same function works on any dataset. Fuel efficiency by number of cylinders in mtcars:

analyze_data(mtcars, "cyl", "mpg")
# A tibble: 3 × 3
    cyl mean_value sd_value
  <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1     4       26.7     4.51
2     6       19.7     1.45
3     8       15.1     2.56

Passing bare column names with { }

If you would rather call the function with bare names, like you do with dplyr itself, wrap the arguments in double curly braces (dplyr calls this “embracing”):

analyze_data2 <- function(data, group_col, num_col) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ group_col }}) |>
    summarize(
      mean_value = mean({{ num_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_value = sd({{ num_col }}, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

analyze_data2(mtcars, cyl, mpg)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
    cyl mean_value sd_value
  <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1     4       26.7     4.51
2     6       19.7     1.45
3     8       15.1     2.56

Use .data[[ ]] when the column names come as text, for example from a vector of names you loop over. Use { } when you want the function to feel like a normal dplyr verb.

Common mistakes

  • “could not find function”. You called the function before running the chunk that defines it. Run the definition first; in a new R session you have to run it again.
  • Using objects from outside the function. If the body refers to a data frame that is not one of the arguments, the function only works in the script where that object happens to exist. Pass everything the function needs as an argument.
  • Reusing a common name. Calling your own function mean or c, or a data frame data, hides R’s own version and leads to confusing errors. That is why the example dataset above is called scores.
  • Expecting more than the last value back. Only the last value (or what you pass to return()) comes out. If you need several results, return a list or a data frame, as in Example 1.

Recap

A function is a named piece of code with inputs (arguments) and an output (the return value). You create one with function(), give arguments defaults with =, and get results back from the last line or from return(). Objects created inside a function stay inside it. Once you notice yourself pasting the same block a third time, that block is a good candidate for a function, and the examples above show how far one short function can take you: from one column to many, and from one dataset to any dataset.

The functions in this post trust their inputs. Give calc_stats() a column that does not exist and it fails with a confusing message. The next post, Error Handling in R, shows how to add checks so your functions fail early with a message that says what went wrong.

item.title: Web Scraping in R: Import table directly from website
item.dc:creator: Gutama Girja Urago
item.description:
Plenty of useful data sits in tables on web pages. The slow way to get it into R is to select the table in your browser, paste it into Excel, fix the formatting, save it as a CSV and then read the CSV. It works, but it takes time, and every manual step is a chance to drop a row or paste into the wrong cell. When the page is updated, you have to do it all again.

The rvest package (say “harvest”) reads a web page straight into R and turns its tables into data frames. In this post we use it to pull Ethiopia’s GDP history from Worldometers, clean the numbers, and draw two charts.

NoteWhat you will learn
  • how to check whether a website is happy for you to scrape it
  • what HTML is and how CSS selectors point at parts of a page
  • how to read a page and extract its tables with rvest
  • how to turn text such as “$127,145,000,000” and “−2.1%” into real numbers, including one trap that silently flips signs
  • how to plot the result with ggplot2

Before you scrape: is it allowed?

Scraping means a program, not a person, is reading the website. Before you start, take two minutes to check that the site is fine with that:

  1. Read the robots.txt file. Most websites publish one at the root of the domain, for example www.worldometers.info/robots.txt. It lists the parts of the site that automated tools should stay away from. When I checked Worldometers’ file for this post, it did not block any pages.
  2. Read the terms of use. Worldometers’ disclaimer page does not mention scraping, and the site marks its content “All rights reserved”. Reading a public table for your own analysis or for learning, as we do here, is a common use. Republishing large amounts of the data is a different matter and would need permission.
  3. Be gentle. Download the page once, save what you need, and work from your saved copy. Do not run a scraper in a loop that hits the same page again and again.

One more point: Worldometers republishes figures from the IMF and the World Bank. For a report or a paper, cite and download from the original source. Scraping is a quick way to get started and a good skill to learn, not a replacement for the official data.

Install and load the packages

# install.packages(c("rvest", "janitor", "dplyr", "readr", "stringr", "ggplot2"))  # run once
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

The commented install.packages() line installs everything this post uses. Note that package names go in quotes.

Read the web page

read_html() downloads the page and stores it in R:

gdp_url <- "https://www.worldometers.info/gdp/ethiopia-gdp/"
page <- read_html(gdp_url)
page
{html_document}
<html data-astro-transition-scope="astro-m2otfycz-2" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="highcharts-light">
[1] <head>\n<meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=UTF-8 ...
[2] <body class="font-body text-base">\n<div class="flex flex-col" data-wm-pa ...

What you see is the start of the page’s HTML, the language web pages are written in. An HTML page is a set of nested elements, each marked with a tag: <head> holds information about the page, <body> holds what you see, <p> is a paragraph, and <table> is a table. Our data is inside one of the <table> elements.

Finding the table: CSS selectors

To tell rvest which part of the page you want, you use a CSS selector, a short pattern that matches elements. The three you will use most often are:

Selector Matches Example
table every element with that tag all tables on the page
.name (dot first) every element with that class .table matches elements with class="table"
#name (hash first) the one element with that id #gdp matches id="gdp"

To see the tags, classes and ids behind a page, open it in Chrome or Firefox, right-click the table and choose Inspect. The developer tools open and highlight the HTML for the element you clicked. As you move the mouse over the code, the matching part of the page lights up.

When I first wrote this post in 2024, the table had the class table, so the selector was .table. Worldometers has since redesigned the page. That is a normal hazard of scraping: a selector that depends on a class name breaks when the designers rename the class. Here we use the tag selector table instead, which matches every table on the page whatever its class.

Extract the tables

html_elements() finds all elements that match a selector, and html_table() turns each HTML table into a data frame:

table_nodes <- html_elements(page, "table")
tables <- html_table(table_nodes)

length(tables)
[1] 5

The page has several tables, so tables is a list of data frames. Before picking one, look at the column names of each:

lapply(tables, names)
[[1]]
[1] "Year"                      "GDP Nominal (Current USD)"
[3] "GDP Growth"                "GDP per capita"           
[5] "Pop. Change"              

[[2]]
[1] "Year"                  "GDP PPP"               "GDP PPP per Capita"   
[4] "PPP Per Capita Change" "Pop. Change"          

[[3]]
[1] "Year"                                   
[2] "GDP Nominal (Current USD)"              
[3] "GDP Real (Constant, Inflation Adjusted)"
[4] "Pop. Change"                            

[[4]]
[1] "Year"                      "GDP Nominal (Current USD)"
[3] "GDP Growth"                "GDP per capita"           
[5] "Pop. Change"              

[[5]]
[1] "Year"                  "GDP PPP"               "GDP PPP per Capita"   
[4] "PPP Per Capita Change" "Pop. Change"

The first table has the yearly figures we want: nominal GDP, GDP growth, GDP per capita and population change. We take it out of the list with double brackets:

gdp_raw <- tables[[1]]
gdp_raw
# A tibble: 47 × 5
    Year `GDP Nominal (Current USD)` `GDP Growth` `GDP per capita` `Pop. Change`
   <int> <chr>                       <chr>        <chr>            <chr>        
 1  2026 $127,145,000,000            9.2%         $1,131           +2.53%       
 2  2025 $126,351,000,000            9.2%         $1,142           +2.58%       
 3  2024 $210,000,000,000            8.1%         $1,937           +2.62%       
 4  2023 $163,709,000,000            7.2%         $1,549           +2.64%       
 5  2022 $126,770,000,000            6.4%         $1,218           +2.66%       
 6  2021 $111,266,000,000            6.3%         $1,092           +2.71%       
 7  2020 $107,672,000,000            6.1%         $1,080           +2.75%       
 8  2019 $95,945,000,000             9.0%         $983             +2.73%       
 9  2018 $84,298,000,000             7.7%         $883             +2.73%       
10  2017 $81,788,000,000             10.2%        $876             +2.76%       
# ℹ 37 more rows

If Worldometers reorders its tables in future, the lapply(tables, names) output tells you which number to use instead of 1.

Clean the data

The table looks right, but R does not see numbers yet:

glimpse(gdp_raw)
Rows: 47
Columns: 5
$ Year                        <int> 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, 2021, 2020, …
$ `GDP Nominal (Current USD)` <chr> "$127,145,000,000", "$126,351,000,000", "$…
$ `GDP Growth`                <chr> "9.2%", "9.2%", "8.1%", "7.2%", "6.4%", "6…
$ `GDP per capita`            <chr> "$1,131", "$1,142", "$1,937", "$1,549", "$…
$ `Pop. Change`               <chr> "+2.53%", "+2.58%", "+2.62%", "+2.64%", "+…

Every column except Year is stored as text (<chr>), because the values contain dollar signs, commas, percent signs and plus signs. We also have column names with spaces and brackets, which are awkward to type in R. Two steps fix this.

Step 1: tidy the column names

clean_names() from the janitor package converts names to lower case with underscores, so “GDP Nominal (Current USD)” becomes gdp_nominal_current_usd:

gdp <- janitor::clean_names(gdp_raw)
names(gdp)
[1] "year"                    "gdp_nominal_current_usd"
[3] "gdp_growth"              "gdp_per_capita"         
[5] "pop_change"

Step 2: turn text into numbers (and avoid a sign trap)

parse_number() from readr reads the number out of a piece of text and ignores symbols around it. It handles dollar signs, commas and percent signs. There is one catch, though. Worldometers writes negative growth with the typographic minus sign “−” (Unicode U+2212), not the ordinary hyphen “-” on your keyboard. They look almost the same, but parse_number() only understands the hyphen, and it drops the other one without telling you:

parse_number("-2.1%")         # ordinary hyphen
[1] -2.1
parse_number("−2.1%")    # typographic minus: the sign is lost
[1] 2.1

The second result is 2.1, a positive number. If we did not catch this, every year of negative growth would turn into positive growth in our charts. So we write a small function that first swaps the typographic minus for a hyphen and then parses the number:

to_number <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(as.character(x), "−", "-")
  parse_number(x)
}

to_number(c("$127,145,000,000", "9.2%", "+2.53%", "−2.1%"))
[1]  1.27145e+11  9.20000e+00  2.53000e+00 -2.10000e+00

Now apply it to every column at once with across():

gdp <- gdp |>
  mutate(across(everything(), to_number))

glimpse(gdp)
Rows: 47
Columns: 5
$ year                    <dbl> 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, 2021, 2020, 2019…
$ gdp_nominal_current_usd <dbl> 1.27145e+11, 1.26351e+11, 2.10000e+11, 1.63709…
$ gdp_growth              <dbl> 9.2, 9.2, 8.1, 7.2, 6.4, 6.3, 6.1, 9.0, 7.7, 1…
$ gdp_per_capita          <dbl> 1131, 1142, 1937, 1549, 1218, 1092, 1080, 983,…
$ pop_change              <dbl> 2.53, 2.58, 2.62, 2.64, 2.66, 2.71, 2.75, 2.73…

mutate(across(everything(), to_number)) means “for every column, replace its values with to_number() of those values”. All columns are now numeric (<dbl>).

Check the result

Cleaning steps can go wrong without any error, as the minus sign just showed. A quick check against the website is always worth it. Here are the years with negative growth; compare them with the page:

gdp |>
  filter(gdp_growth < 0) |>
  select(year, gdp_growth)
# A tibble: 7 × 2
   year gdp_growth
  <dbl>      <dbl>
1  2003       -2.1
2  1998       -4.2
3  1992       -8.9
4  1991       -7.2
5  1989       -0.5
6  1985      -11.4
7  1984       -2.3

If this returns no rows while the website shows some negative years, the minus signs were lost somewhere. A cell that was empty on the website shows up as NA, which is what we want.

Finally, save a copy so you do not need to download the page again every time you work on the analysis:

write_csv(gdp, "ethiopia_gdp_worldometers.csv")

Plot nominal GDP

With clean numbers, ggplot2 needs only a few lines:

gdp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = gdp_nominal_current_usd)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B")) +
  labs(
    title = "Ethiopia's nominal GDP (current US dollars)",
    subtitle = paste0(min(gdp$year), " to ", max(gdp$year)),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Nominal GDP",
    caption = "Source: Worldometers, based on IMF data"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

A few things worth knowing:

  • aes(x = year, y = gdp_nominal_current_usd) maps the columns to the axes. Because year is a number, ggplot2 spaces the years correctly and picks sensible tick marks for us.
  • scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B") divides the values by one billion and shows them as “$100B” instead of “100000000000”.
  • The subtitle is built from the data with min() and max(), so it stays correct when the website adds a new year.

Nominal GDP in US dollars moves with the exchange rate as well as with the economy. If you see a sharp drop in the most recent years, the likely cause is Ethiopia’s move to a market-based exchange rate for the birr in 2024. Check the growth chart below: if growth stayed positive in those years, the economy did not shrink, and the drop comes from converting birr into dollars at a new rate.

Plot GDP growth

The second chart shows yearly growth, with positive and negative years in different colours:

gdp |>
  filter(!is.na(gdp_growth)) |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(gdp_growth >= 0, "Growth", "Decline")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = gdp_growth, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Growth = "#2E8B57", Decline = "#C0392B")) +
  labs(
    title = "Ethiopia's GDP growth (%)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "GDP growth (%)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Worldometers, based on IMF data"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
  • filter(!is.na(gdp_growth)) drops the year with no growth value, so ggplot2 does not warn about it.
  • if_else() labels each year “Growth” or “Decline”, and fill = direction colours the bars by that label.
  • scale_fill_manual() sets the two colours by name.

This is the chart where the minus-sign fix matters. Without it, the decline years would show as green bars.

Scraping politely with the polite package

For anything beyond a single page, have a look at the polite package. It reads robots.txt for you, introduces itself to the website, and waits between requests. The code is almost the same as before:

library(polite)

session <- bow(gdp_url, user_agent = "GDP tutorial by Gutama Girja Urago")
page <- scrape(session)

bow() checks that you are allowed to visit the page, and scrape() downloads it. The rest of the post works unchanged.

Common mistakes

  • The selector returns nothing. html_elements() gives an empty result when nothing matches. Inspect the page again: the class or id may have changed, as it did for this page.
  • Picking the wrong table. A page often has several tables. Check lapply(tables, names) before choosing one by number.
  • Numbers that are still text. If a column shows <chr> in glimpse(), it has not been converted. Plotting it gives odd results, and arithmetic fails.
  • Silent changes to values. Look-alike characters, such as the typographic minus here or thin spaces in large numbers, can change values without any error. Always compare a few cleaned values with the website.
  • Pages built by JavaScript. Some sites load their tables after the page opens. read_html() only sees the original HTML, so those tables will be missing. In that case, look for a download button or an API instead.

Recap

Check robots.txt and the terms of use, then read the page with read_html(), find the tables with html_elements() and turn them into data frames with html_table(). Clean the column names with janitor::clean_names() and convert text to numbers with parse_number(), after replacing any typographic minus signs. Check a few values against the website, save a local copy, and plot. The same steps work for most tables you find on the web. The two parts that change from site to site are the selector and the cleaning.

Back to top

item.title: Table Template: Create your own {gt} table theme
item.dc:creator: Gutama Girja Urago
item.description:
Most analysis ends with a table: summary statistics for a report, balance checks for an evaluation, a results table for a paper. R prints data frames in the console just fine, but those printouts are not something you would paste into a report. The gt package turns a data frame into a clean, formatted table that you can put in a Quarto document, a web page or a Word file.

In this post we build a table step by step, one layer of styling at a time, and then wrap all the steps into a single function. Once you have that function, every table in your report can have the same look with one line of code. The post was inspired by this video tutorial.

NoteWhat you will learn
  • the parts of a gt table and what each one is called
  • how tab_style() works: what to change and where to change it
  • how to add a title, striped rows, column group labels (spanners) and a source note
  • how to turn your styling into a reusable theme function

Setting up

You need two packages: gt for the table and dplyr to prepare the data. If you have never installed them, run the install.packages() line once (it is commented out here so it does not reinstall every time).

# install.packages(c("gt", "dplyr"))   # run once if needed
library(gt)
library(dplyr)

The parts of a gt table

gt names each part of a table, and you will use these names when you style it. From top to bottom:

  • Header: the title and an optional subtitle.
  • Column labels: the names above each column.
  • Spanners: labels that sit above a group of related columns, such as “Sepal” above “Length” and “Width”.
  • Body: the rows of data.
  • Footer: source notes and footnotes under the table.

Keep this list in mind. Almost every gt function either adds one of these parts or changes how one of them looks.

Prepare the data

We use R’s built-in iris dataset, which has flower measurements for three species of iris. To keep the table short, we take the first two rows of each species:

iris_sample <- iris |>
  mutate(Species = stringr::str_to_title(Species)) |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  slice_head(n = 2) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Species, everything())

iris_sample
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  Species    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
  <chr>             <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Setosa              5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2
2 Setosa              4.9         3            1.4         0.2
3 Versicolor          7           3.2          4.7         1.4
4 Versicolor          6.4         3.2          4.5         1.5
5 Virginica           6.3         3.3          6           2.5
6 Virginica           5.8         2.7          5.1         1.9

What each step does:

  • mutate(Species = stringr::str_to_title(Species)) capitalises the species names, so “setosa” becomes “Setosa”. The stringr:: prefix lets us use one function from the stringr package without loading the whole package.
  • group_by(Species) and slice_head(n = 2) keep the first two rows of each species. ungroup() removes the grouping again so it does not affect later steps.
  • select(Species, everything()) moves Species to the first column and keeps all the others after it.

Your first gt table

Turning a data frame into a gt table takes one function:

tbl <- gt(iris_sample)
tbl
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

This already looks better than the console output. Each of the steps below takes tbl, adds one thing to it with the pipe |>, and saves the result back into tbl. That way you can run the post chunk by chunk and watch the table change.

Add a header

tab_header() adds a title and a subtitle above the table:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Main Title",
    subtitle = "Subtitle"
  )

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

In a real report, the title says what the table shows (“Iris measurements by species”) and the subtitle adds detail (“First two plants of each species, in cm”).

How styling works: tab_style()

Before we change any colours, it helps to see how gt thinks about style. tab_style() always takes two arguments:

  • style: what to change. Helper functions describe it, for example cell_text() for the font, cell_fill() for the background colour and cell_borders() for the lines.
  • locations: where to change it. Another set of helpers points at a part of the table: cells_title(), cells_column_labels(), cells_column_spanners(), cells_body() and so on, matching the parts listed earlier.

So “make the title bold” becomes “style = bold text, location = the title”.

Style the title

Here we make the title black and bold. cells_title(groups = "title") points at the title only, so the subtitle keeps its normal style:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  )

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

To style the subtitle instead, you would use groups = "subtitle".

Stripe the rows

Shading every other row makes a wide table easier to read across. We give odd-numbered rows a light grey background:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "grey90"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = seq(1, nrow(iris_sample), by = 2))
  )

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

seq(1, nrow(iris_sample), by = 2) produces the row numbers 1, 3, 5 and so on, up to the number of rows in the data. Using nrow() instead of typing the numbers means this still works if you change how many rows you keep.

Adjust table options

tab_options() controls settings that apply to the whole table. Here we stretch the table to the full width of the page, give the column labels a blue background, and left-align the title:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    column_labels.background.color = "steelblue",
    heading.align = "left"
  )

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

pct(100) means 100 percent of the available width. gt has over a hundred options like these; the tab_options() reference page lists them all.

Group columns with spanners

The iris column names contain a pattern: Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length and Petal.Width. The part before the dot is the flower part and the part after it is the measurement. tab_spanner_delim() splits each name at a delimiter (here the dot) and turns the first part into a spanner above the columns:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_spanner_delim(delim = ".")

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species
Sepal
Petal
Length Width Length Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

The four columns are now grouped under “Sepal” and “Petal”, and each column label is just “Length” or “Width”. The table is easier to read and narrower.

Make the labels stand out

Finally, we make the column labels bold and the spanners bold and a little larger:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold", size = "medium"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  )

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species
Sepal
Petal
Length Width Length Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9

Two tab_style() calls are chained with |> here: one for the labels and one for the spanners.

Add a source note

A table in a report should say where its numbers come from. tab_source_note() adds a line to the footer:

tbl <- tbl |>
  tab_source_note(source_note = "Source: R's built-in iris dataset.")

tbl
Main Title
Subtitle
Species
Sepal
Petal
Length Width Length Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5
Virginica 5.8 2.7 5.1 1.9
Source: R's built-in iris dataset.

Make it reusable

We now have a table we like, but it took eight steps. Copying those steps for every table in a report would be slow, and the tables would drift apart as you tweak one and forget the others. A function solves this. (If functions are new to you, my post on R functions covers the basics.)

my_gt_theme <- function(gt_table, title, subtitle = NULL, delim = ".") {
  gt_table |>
    tab_header(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold"),
      locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
    ) |>
    opt_row_striping() |>
    tab_options(
      row.striping.background_color = "grey90",
      table.width = pct(100),
      column_labels.background.color = "steelblue",
      heading.align = "left"
    ) |>
    tab_spanner_delim(delim = delim) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
      locations = cells_column_labels()
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(weight = "bold", size = "medium"),
      locations = cells_column_spanners()
    )
}

This is the same set of steps as above, with three changes worth pointing out:

  • The first argument is a gt table. That means the function fits into a pipe: gt(data) |> my_gt_theme(...), just like gt’s own functions.
  • Row striping uses opt_row_striping(). Earlier we picked the odd rows ourselves with nrow(). Inside a function that receives a gt table, it is simpler to switch on gt’s built-in striping and set its colour in tab_options(). The result looks the same.
  • subtitle and delim have defaults. subtitle = NULL means “no subtitle” unless you give one, and delim = "." matches the iris column names. You only need to supply them when you want something different.

Now the whole table takes one line:

gt(iris_sample) |>
  my_gt_theme(
    title = "Easy and Beautiful Theme",
    subtitle = "With very minimal code"
  )
Easy and Beautiful Theme
With very minimal code
Species
Sepal
Petal
Length Width Length Width
Setosa 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2
Setosa 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2
Versicolor 7.0 3.2 4.7 1.4
Versicolor 6.4 3.2 4.5 1.5
Virginica 6.3 3.3 6.0 2.5

Saving your table

To use the table outside R, save it with gtsave(). The file extension decides the format:

final_table <- gt(iris_sample) |>
  my_gt_theme(title = "Iris measurements", subtitle = "First two plants per species")

gtsave(final_table, "iris_table.html")   # web page
gtsave(final_table, "iris_table.docx")   # Word document

Saving as an image (.png) also works, but needs the webshot2 package and a Chrome browser on your computer.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to save the result. tbl |> tab_header(...) prints a table with a header, but tbl itself does not change unless you write tbl <- tbl |> ....
  • Wrong location helper. Styling column labels with cells_body() (or the other way round) runs without error but changes the wrong part of the table. Check which part you mean against the list at the top.
  • Spanners that do not appear. tab_spanner_delim() only works when the column names actually contain the delimiter. If yours use _ instead of ., pass delim = "_".
  • Hard-coded row numbers. rows = c(1, 3, 5) gives the wrong stripes, without any warning, as soon as the number of rows changes. Use seq() with nrow(), or opt_row_striping().

Recap

A gt table is built in layers: header, column labels, spanners, body and footer. tab_header(), tab_spanner_delim() and tab_source_note() add parts, tab_style() changes how a part looks by combining a style with a location, and tab_options() sets table-wide options. Once you are happy with a look, put the steps in a function that takes a gt table as its first argument. From then on, every table in your report gets the same style with one line, and changing the style means changing one function.
